rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Stars serve human travelers, so deifying them is foolish; their service to earth's people shows one God governs both heaven and earth and merits gratitude and worship.
rows.anchor: they are serving the needs of those who live on the earth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab poets describe stars both as guides on night journeys and as markers of the hours of night, making them travel guides and clocks.
rows.anchor: they serve both as clocks and as travel guides.

rows.speaker: the Arabs
rows.claim: Arabs worshipped some stars, including Sirius (shi‘rā), which appears in spring; they also treated some stars as auspicious and others as ill-omened.
rows.anchor: the Arabs also worshipped certain stars. Thus, Sirius ( shi‘rā) has been referred to by the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here āyāt means signs and, because a sign proves what it signifies, also proofs and arguments.
rows.anchor: Here it means “signs” and since every sign is a proof of the thing it is a sign of, it also means “proofs” and “arguments.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs supply arguments chiefly for monotheism and also for the hereafter and prophethood; each sign has several aspects, while its referent is left for the curious audience to discern.
rows.anchor: As monotheism is mentioned here and secondarily the hereafter and prophethood too are mentioned, it would here mean arguments and proofs about them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against Quraysh's demand for a tangible miracle, the passage points to signs that satisfy intellect and heart; those who seek only the palpable remain blind even when miracles appear.
rows.anchor: if they want to see miracles, then God has stated signs that satisfy the intellect and the heart.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means people who want to know: sometimes a verb expresses the intention behind an action.
rows.anchor: At times a verb is used to connote its intention. For this reason, the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anshaʾa means not only to create but also to make someone grow and develop.
rows.anchor: used here does not merely mean “to create,” it also means to make someone grow and develop.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The single being is Adam, regarded by all divine religions as humanity's father; the Arabs also accepted this.
rows.anchor: The “single being” refers to Adam (sws) who is regarded by all divine religions as the father of mankind.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spouse came from the same kind, and despite outward and linguistic diversity, shared natural needs and male-female harmony show one Creator and a common purpose rather than separate deities and ancestors.
rows.anchor: all of human beings have the same instinctive and natural needs. This is proof of the fact that all of them have the same creator.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God founded human society on one ancestor and one Creator; those who attack this foundation are criminals who spread anarchy on earth.
rows.anchor: It is on this unity of ancestor and unity of creator that God has founded the human society

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening verse of al-Nisāʾ states the same premise: humanity was made from one soul and its mate, and blood ties must be respected.
rows.anchor: Its very first verse presents this premise thus:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mustaqarr means a resting place and here indicates the place where a person lives after birth.
rows.anchor: Concomitant indications show that the former means the place where a person lives when he is born.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about a place to live and benefit from resources until a set time in al-Baqarah supports this sense of mustaqarr.
rows.anchor: are used in verse 36 of Sūrah al-Baqarah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mustawdaʿ means a person's place of burial.
rows.anchor: The latter word means a person’s place of burial.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People live for their allotted days and use assigned resources under God's watch and knowledge; their life and burial place are both known to Him.
rows.anchor: This life of a human being and using these resources shows that he is watched over by God and is in His knowledge.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that God knows a person's dwelling and burial echoes Hūd 11:6, which says every creature's provision and abode are known and recorded by God.
rows.anchor: Thus in verse 6 of Sūrah Hūd, it is said:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God provides people with their means after birth, they should not take someone else as guardian and protector.
rows.anchor: if after birth human beings receive the means and resources of sustaining themselves from God, why should they regard someone else to be their guardian and protector?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the burial place a deposit subtly signals resurrection: the dead are entrusted to earth, then raised for reward for gratitude or punishment for ingratitude; this providence follows from God's knowledge and wisdom.
rows.anchor: when people die, they are not obliterated; they are in fact entrusted to the earth from where they will be extracted and rewarded for their gratitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated statement that signs are fully explained marks stubborn addressees who demand a miracle as an excuse not to understand.
rows.anchor: The words “We have fully explained Our signs to those who understand” also occur earlier.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowledge concerns the intellect while understanding concerns the heart; the latter recalls al-Aʿrāf's statement that people have hearts that do not understand.
rows.anchor: The difference between “knowledge” and “understanding” is that the former relates to the intellect and the latter to the heart.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those enslaved to what is observable are like donkeys, which understand only the use of force.
rows.anchor: he is exemplified by a donkey which only understands the use of force.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Intellect and heart reach God by observing the universe and looking beyond what is palpable; fixation on immediate gains makes people see details but miss the greater reality and understand nothing.
rows.anchor: at times he may see a mole but is unable to see the mountain behind it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage now turns to signs of God's mercy, providence, power, wisdom, and oneness, which also testify to the hereafter and are visible to those willing to believe.
rows.anchor: Attention is now directed to the signs and arguments that depict God’s mercy, providence, power, wisdom and His oneness as well as testify to the hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-samāʾ can mean either sky or clouds.
rows.anchor: means “sky” as well as “clouds.”

words: أَنزَلَ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ مَاءًۭ فَأَخْرَجْنَا بِهِۦ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The speaker first remains unspecified and is then identified as God, expressing care and providence and showing that God rules heaven, earth, air, and clouds as one realm.
rows.anchor: the verse began with the speaker not being specified and then it was specified as God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain falling from heaven and drawing out the earth's treasures displays harmony under one ruler; reviving dead land by rain is Qur'anic evidence that resurrection is possible.
rows.anchor: the revival of dead land as a result of rain is presented as evidence of the hereafter.

words: فَأَخْرَجْنَا مِنْهُ خَضِرًۭا نُّخْرِجُ مِنْهُ حَبًّۭا مُّتَرَاكِبًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grain illustrates a specific form of providence after the general one; it is mentioned first because it is commonly needed and can be stored, prompting reflection on a wise and powerful Creator.
rows.anchor: First grains are mentioned since they are commonly needed and can also be stored.

words: وَمِنَ ٱلنَّخْلِ مِن طَلْعِهَا قِنْوَانٌۭ دَانِيَةٌۭ وَجَنَّٰتٍۢ مِّنْ أَعْنَابٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verbs are omitted in both linked clauses about dates and orchards; the first omitted verb is passive and the second active.
rows.anchor: The first is a passive verb and the second, an active one.

words: وَمِنَ ٱلنَّخْلِ مِن طَلْعِهَا قِنْوَانٌۭ دَانِيَةٌۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dates were a staple Arab fruit, and the verse traces their development from tree and buds to heavy hanging clusters so people can witness God's creativity and infer His power, wisdom, mercy, and providence.
rows.anchor: attention is focused on their trees, on buds being created in these trees and from these buds heavy hanging bunches coming into being

words: وَمِنَ ٱلنَّخْلِ مِن طَلْعِهَا قِنْوَانٌۭ دَانِيَةٌۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who see nature's elements sustain a date tree still foolishly imagine the world as a contest among many deities and competing intentions.
rows.anchor: all elements of nature look after it but they still foolishly believe that this world is the battle-field of many deities and intents.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some enjoy God's provisions as if they existed only for food and comfort, never asking what responsibility they owe their provider or whether they will answer for these favors.
rows.anchor: It is as if they enjoy privileges but have no obligation towards them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grapes, olives, and pomegranates are named because they were common in Arabia; the point is that people received fruits as well as staple food.
rows.anchor: The purpose of their mention is not just to point to a few specific fruits for they are only mentioned because they were very common in Arabia.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fruit varieties resemble and differ from one another in appearance, size, and taste, reflecting God's providence, mercy, power, wisdom, and generosity.
rows.anchor: each has different varieties which are similar to one another and others which are different from one another in appearance, size and taste.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People could survive on bread and water, so abundant fruit that delights taste and smell manifests the Creator's generosity and is meant to awaken purification and innate gratitude, religion's foundation.
rows.anchor: Why then did the creator create for them all kinds of fruits in such abundance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun's antecedent is all the items mentioned, but its singular form directs attention to each item individually; a word meaning ripening is elided after the reference to ripening.
rows.anchor: The pronoun occurs in the singular so that it points to each of these things separately and directs people to reflect on each of them.

words: ٱنظُرُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ ثَمَرِهِۦٓ إِذَآ أَثْمَرَ وَيَنْعِهِۦٓ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reflecting on every stage from inception to ripening reveals countless signs; each branch, flower, and fruit is a miracle for those demanding a sign.
rows.anchor: If they have eyes, each branch, each flower and each fruit is no less than a miracle.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The world could have survived in a plain, monotonous form, but its myriad petals and flowers were made to disclose God's power, wisdom, mercy, and providence so people could know Him.
rows.anchor: This world did not need all these marvels and majesties for its survival.
